1.title: Security and Safety
1.text: Welcome to Module fifteen: Security and Safety. It covers the exam area Part five: Automation and safety. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do seven things. Keep secrets out of a repository with dot git ignore and environment variables. Respond to a committed secret by rotating, amending, rewriting history and force pushing. Find a secret with git log dash S. Explain secret scanning, push protection and Depend a bot. Sign commits with an S S H key and verify them. Harden a workflow by pinning actions, limiting permissions and avoiding script injection. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: What Was Executed and What Is Reference Only
1.text: What Was Executed and What Is Reference Only. The signing, history and secret examples were run for real in practice repositories. Git Hub's secret scanning, push protection and Depend a bot come from the official Git Hub documentation and were not run.

1.title: Keep secrets out of the repository
1.text: Keep secrets out of the repository. A secret is anything that grants access: a token, an A P I key, a private key, a login. Git remembers everything, so a secret committed once lives in the history of every clone. The figure shows the layers of defense.

1.title: Keep secrets out of the repository, continued
1.text: Keep secrets out of the repository. The figure shows this: Four layers of defense: keep secrets out of commits, scan and block pushes, sign commits, and harden the workflows that run your code.

1.title: Keep secrets out of the repository, continued
1.text: Keep secrets out of the repository. Read secrets from environment variables. Write secrets in code, config files, commit messages or issues. Keep local values in a dot env file that dot git ignore lists. Commit dot env; commit a dot env dot example with fake placeholders instead. Keep shared values in a secret store, such as Actions secrets. Put a token in a remote U R L: it is saved as plain text in dot git slash config. dot git ignore only affects files that Git does not track yet. A file that is already tracked stays tracked until you run git rm the cached flag on it. Tip: Add dot env to dot git ignore before the first commit, and commit a dot env dot example with fake values. New teammates learn the variable names and never see a real secret.

1.title: A secret was committed: rotate first
1.text: A secret was committed: rotate first. The order matters. Rotate the credential first: create a new one and revoke the old one at the service that issued it. Only then clean the history. A secret that reached a shared repository must be treated as leaked, because clones, forks and caches keep copies even after you delete it.

1.title: A secret was committed: rotate first, continued
1.text: A secret was committed: rotate first. Last commit, not pushed. git rm the cached flag the file, then git commit the amend flag. Older commit, or already pushed. Rewrite every commit with git filter repo or the B F G Repo-Cleaner, then force push with the force with lease flag; teammates must re-clone or reset. Pushed to a shared repository. Rotate anyway: rewriting history is cleanup, not a cure. To find a secret, git log dash S text lists the commits that add or remove that exact text. Try it: the last commit added dot env with a fake key. Your hashes will differ.

1.title: A secret was committed: rotate first, continued
1.text: A secret was committed: rotate first. The output is trimmed: the amend prints more lines, and the second search prints nothing because the branch no longer holds the key. The old commit still sits in the reflog (module six), which the last command reads, and on any clone that already fetched it. That is why the rotation comes first. Tip: Rotate the credential before you touch the history. Cleaning takes time, and a leaked key can be used the whole time.

1.title: What GitHub adds: scanning, protection, Dependabot, signing
1.text: What Git Hub adds: scanning, protection, Depend a bot, signing. Secret scanning. What it does: Scans the full history of every branch, and also issues, pull requests, discussions and wikis. Good to know: Free for public repositories; private and internal organization repositories need Git Hub Secret Protection. Push protection. What it does: Blocks a push that contains a detected secret. Good to know: For users, on by default in public repositories; for repositories it needs Git Hub Secret Protection and is off by default.

1.title: What GitHub adds: scanning, protection, Dependabot, signing, continued
1.text: What Git Hub adds: scanning, protection, Depend a bot, signing. Depend a bot alerts. What it does: Warn about vulnerable dependencies when a new advisory is added or the dependency graph changes. Good to know: Scan the default branch; admins and organization owners enable them. Depend a bot version updates. What it does: Open pull requests that keep dependencies and actions current. Good to know: You choose what to watch.

1.title: What GitHub adds: scanning, protection, Dependabot, signing, continued
1.text: What Git Hub adds: scanning, protection, Depend a bot, signing. Anyone with write access can override a push protection block by default, and must give a reason. "It's used in tests" and "It's a false positive" create closed alerts; "I'll fix it later" creates an open alert. When an alert names a real credential, rotate it. Depend a bot alerts for Actions cover only semantic versions, not S H A pins.

1.title: What GitHub adds: scanning, protection, Dependabot, signing, continued
1.text: What Git Hub adds: scanning, protection, Depend a bot, signing. Signed commits prove who made a commit. Git can sign with G P G, S or M I M E or, since Git two point three four, an S S H key. Git Hub shows a Verified badge when it can check the signature, and Unverified when it cannot; an unsigned commit shows no status. A branch protection rule can require signed commits. Commits made in the web interface are signed by Git Hub itself, but ree base and merge commits are not.

1.title: What GitHub adds: scanning, protection, Dependabot, signing, continued
1.text: What Git Hub adds: scanning, protection, Depend a bot, signing. The empty dash N means no protection for the private key, and the key sits next to the code: both are only for this lab. In real life keep the key in your dot ssh folder, protect it with a phrase and add its public half to your Git Hub account. The allowed signers file lists whom your local Git trusts, and verify commit fails without it. Tip: Turn on push protection. Blocking a secret before the push is far cheaper than rotating it and cleaning the history afterwards.

2.title: Safer Actions and token hygiene
2.text: Safer Actions and token hygiene. A workflow runs code with access to your repository, so a careless line can leak a secret or run an attacker's code. Third-party actions. Pin to a full commit S H A, because a tag can be moved; a tag is fine only for creators you trust. Token rights. Least privilege: read contents by default and raise it per job. Untrusted text. Never write github dot event dot pull request dot title inside run; Git Hub pastes it into the script text, so a title can add commands. Hand it over through env.

2.title: Safer Actions and token hygiene, continued
2.text: Safer Actions and token hygiene. pull request target. Runs in the context of the base repository, so avoid it unless needed and never check out the pull request code under it. Self-hosted runners. Almost never on public repositories. Cloud credentials. Prefer O I D C to long-lived keys. Changes to workflows. code owners can require review for dot github slash workflows; Depend a bot version updates keep pinned actions current.

2.title: Safer Actions and token hygiene, continued
2.text: Safer Actions and token hygiene. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

2.title: Safer Actions and token hygiene, continued
2.text: Safer Actions and token hygiene. Token hygiene. Prefer a fine-grained personal access token: one owner, only the repositories it needs and granular permissions. A classic token with the repo scope reaches every repository you can reach. Keep tokens out of remote U R Ls, scripts and chats. Let S S H or a credential helper such as Git Credential Manager hold them, and use the short-lived github token inside workflows. Revoke tokens you no longer use.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. You committed dot env with a live A P I key as your last commit and have not pushed. What is the best first step? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Rotate the key at the service, then fix the commit. A secret that was committed must be rotated first, because the old commit may still be copied or read.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A key was pushed to main yesterday and teammates pulled it. You amend, force push and delete the file. Is the key safe now? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: No, clones and forks may still hold the old commit. Copies of a pushed commit can live in clones, forks and caches, so the key must be treated as leaked and rotated.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. git log dash S demo-nine f eight e seven d six c the oneline flag prints two commits: nine c two e four one a Remove key and four b seven d zero f three Add config. What does this show? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: The text was added in one commit and removed in the other. dash S lists commits that add or remove the text, so the key is still in the history.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. With gpg dot format ssh and a signing key set, git verify commit head fails with an error about a missing file. What is missing? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: A gpg dot ssh dot allowed Signers File that lists the trusted keys. Local verification of S S H signatures needs an allowed signers file with the trusted public keys.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A workflow has run echo github dot event dot pull request dot title. A contributor names a pull request with shell commands in it. What is the risk and the fix? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: The title's commands run, so hand it over through env. Git Hub pastes the title into the script text before the shell runs, so values should arrive through an environment variable.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. A workflow uses octo org slash lint action at version two, and the team fears the tag could be moved to bad code. What is the safest change? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Pin the action to a full commit S H A of a reviewed version. A full commit S H A cannot be moved, while tags and branches can.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What do you do first when a secret was pushed? Answer: Rotate the credential at the service that issued it. Question two. Which command lists the commits that add or remove a piece of text? Answer: git log dash S. Question three. Which tools rewrite the history of every commit to remove a file? Answer: git filter repo or the B F G Repo-Cleaner.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Which setting makes Git sign commits with an S S H key? Answer: gpg dot format ssh, together with user dot signingkey. Question five. What does push protection do? Answer: It blocks a push that contains a detected secret. Question six. Which event needs care because it runs in the base repository context? Answer: pull request target.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Keep out: environment variables; dot env in dot git ignore; dot env dot example; secret stores; no tokens in U R Ls. Committed a secret: rotate first; git rm the cached flag and git commit the amend flag for the last commit. Find it: git log dash S text the oneline flag. Git Hub features: secret scanning of full history; push protection blocks pushes; Depend a bot alerts and version updates. Signed commits: gpg dot format ssh, user dot signingkey, commit dot gpgsign, allowed signers file; Verified badge. Actions hardening: pin to a commit S H A; least privilege; no text in run. Tokens: fine-grained over classic; short-lived github token; revoke unused tokens.
